What was measured

Methods

What was measured, on what, and what the results do and do not say. Every number on this site comes from one run of genomic-benchmarks-qc — run {{qc_run}} — rolled up by gb-audit {{package_version}} in run {{audit_run}}.

What a flag is

Each check returns one of {{n_flags_word}} flags on one split: Pass, Warning, Fail, Unknown. The first {{n_scored_flags_word}} are scored outcomes and are ordered by severity. Unknown is not the fourth degree of that order: it means the check ran and could not be scored. A blank — a check with no flag at all — is a third thing again: the check had nothing to run on.

Keeping those apart matters more than it looks. Reading Unknown or a blank as Pass converts an absence of measurement into a reassuring result, which is the single easiest way to make an audit say more than it found. Every figure on this site draws Unknown as a hatch rather than a fourth colour, and draws nothing at all for a blank.

Pass is the narrowest of the {{n_flags_word}}. It says this check did not separate the classes on this split. It does not say the dataset is free of structure a model could use, because a check that did not find something is not evidence there is nothing to find. No combination of the {{n_checks_word}} flags licenses that conclusion either.

The reference split

A dataset ships several splits and a check runs on each of them. The single flag, AUROC and overlap this site quotes per dataset are the values on that dataset's reference split — train for every dataset but one, where the training split is not released and test stands in.

They are not maxima over splits. A maximum would make a dataset with more splits look worse for having been measured more times, and would name no split a reader could go and check. Every figure here names the split its numbers were measured on, and every dataset page shows all splits alongside the reference one.

The {{n_checks_word}} checks

{{n_probe_checks_cap}} probe checks each fit a single sequence feature against the class labels and report the AUROC it reaches. {{n_integrity_checks_cap}} integrity checks count duplicates and unique bases. Those {{n_split_checks_word}} run per split. The leakage scan runs across pairs of splits and counts sequences of one that are also present in the other.

Reading a probe AUROC

A probe is one feature and one fit — sequence length, GC content, a nucleotide or dinucleotide frequency, a per-position profile. The AUROC it reaches is a lower bound on what is recoverable from the sequences: a stronger feature, or a model, may recover more. It is never an upper bound, and a low value is not evidence that a model would also score low.

Across the {{n_probed}} probed datasets the median strongest probe reaches {{median_probe_auroc}}, and {{n_probe_over_0_7}} datasets reach 0.70 or more from a single feature.

The figure below is the strongest probe per dataset, one mark each. Read a mark as a lower bound on what a model could recover from the sequences alone, and the spread as the range this corpus covers rather than as a ranking.

Reading a split overlap

The leakage scan compares two splits and reports, in each direction, the percentage of one split's sequences that were also present in the other. Both directions are shown because the two differ whenever the splits differ in size, and quoting only the larger would describe neither split.

{{n_leakage_scanned}} of {{n_datasets}} datasets were scanned; {{n_leakage_unscanned_cap}} ships a single split and so has no pair to compare. {{n_with_any_leakage}} have at least one sequence in two splits, {{n_leakage_over_50}} have more than half of one split present in another, and {{n_leakage_complete}} have all of it.

The bands below count datasets rather than implying a density, because the structure worth seeing is all at one end: most of the corpus sits in the narrowest band and a handful sit at the top of the range.

Where these numbers come from

The tables under data/ are committed to this repository and carry a SHA-256 each in data/provenance.json. Two of them — the combined class and split results — are also on the Zenodo record, so the committed copy and the published copy are two routes to the same bytes, and the digests are what make that a claim you can check rather than one you have to take.

gb-audit build turns those tables into docs/data/catalogue.json, which is committed and gated in CI. gb-audit render turns that file plus the templates into this site. The site itself is not committed: every number it shows is already diffable in the catalogue, and the HTML adds none of its own. Neither step writes a timestamp, so two builds of one commit produce the same bytes.

The {{n_reports}} reports are fetched separately with gb-audit fetch, which verifies each archive against the digest in data/reports.csv before unpacking it, and records which route the bytes came by.

How this site words things

The wording here is constrained on purpose, and the constraint is checked by a tool rather than remembered. A check reports what it measured; it does not report a cause. So this site says a probe reached an AUROC, not that a dataset is easy; it says sequences were found in two splits, not that a benchmark is unusable. Where a number is a lower bound it is called one every time it appears, and a flag is always named as the tool's output rather than as a judgement about the data.
